## Original problem

I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

BODY
The earlier account is largely right to treat this as coordination under change rather than a character contest. I would keep that frame but add three refinements. First, an agreement about meaning needs an interpretation rule for unforeseen cases, not just a task list. Write down what done means for the few chores that cause repeat disputes, with examples: sink empty, counters clear, bins at curb by 7pm. Add a rule that if the definition is unclear, the person doing the task chooses a reasonable reading but must flag it at the next check-in; hazards and shared costs are not left to individual discretion. Second, make revision routine. Schedules change, so any flatmate can call a ten-minute reset; until the reset, the current plan stands with a named fallback. This prevents silent drift and also prevents one person from reopening every agreement constantly. Third, address avoidance one-to-one, not as a group confrontation. Ask what makes the conversation costly and offer formats: written updates, pairwise talks, a shorter meeting, or a neutral facilitator. Do not treat absence as consent. At the same time, do not let one person's refusal to discuss become a veto over the others' need for a workable flat. If someone will not participate, set a temporary minimum that does not impose new costs unilaterally: each person handles their own dishes, laundry, and room; shared chores follow a visible default rotation or are suspended until agreement, except for health and safety. If standards differ sharply, say so. The person with the higher standard may need to do more, trade other chores, or agree to pay for help; equal minutes are not always the fair answer. Finally, if repeated attempts fail, mediation or a conversation about whether the living arrangement still works is legitimate. The aim is not perfect harmony but fewer repeated disputes and a way to revise the deal when life changes.
COMMITMENTS
I am taking up the claim that this is primarily a coordination and communication problem, but only as a working hypothesis. It would be defeated or complicated if the avoidance turns out to be about fear, resentment, power, or something outside the flat. My proposed next move is a short written charter for the few recurring chores plus a review date, not a comprehensive household ledger. That depends on at least two people being willing to try a low-cost structure, and on no one being unsafe in the conversation. A proposed test: for two to three weeks use a shared note that states chore, done-definition, owner, fallback and review date, and hold a ten-minute check-in; relevance is to see whether ambiguity or follow-through is the main obstacle. Success would be fewer disputes about what was agreed and at least one missed task handled without a fight. If that fails, I would move to one-to-one inquiry about the avoidance, then a neutral facilitator or a discussion about changing the living arrangement; that depends on lease terms, money, willingness, and whether anyone is being harmed. I am not assuming a cleaner is affordable, that all three want to stay, that standards are equal, or that resentment can be waved away. I would not impose paid help or new costs without consent. A criticism to keep in view: a shared board can become surveillance or a moral scoreboard, so it should stay task-focused and be reviewed for whether it reduces or increases tension. Unresolved: what the avoidance means, whether prior agreements already feel punitive, and whether the higher-standard person will accept less, do more, or pay for help. I would retain the earlier commitment to treat absence as information rather than consent.

BODY
Start by reframing the issue: this is less a moral fight about who is lazy and more a coordination failure under changing schedules and ambiguous agreements. The aim is not to win the argument but to make commitments checkable and revisable.

First, separate standards from methods. Agree on what counts as done: dishes washed and put away, bins out before collection, bathroom wiped down weekly. Do not require everyone to do it the same way if the outcome is acceptable.

Second, make agreements observable. A shared note, whiteboard, or simple app should list who, what, by when, and what happens if it is missed. Vague promises like “I’ll do more” are what later become “that isn’t what I meant.” A short weekly or fortnightly check-in, even ten minutes, can catch drift before resentment hardens.

Third, address the avoidance directly but not as an accusation. Speak one-to-one: “I notice you’ve been pulling away from these conversations, and I don’t want to corner you. What would make them easier?” Offer alternatives: written async updates, a shorter meeting, a rotating facilitator, or a neutral third party. Avoidance may be about anxiety, resentment, schedule exhaustion, or feeling outvoted; you do not know until asked.

Fourth, do not let one person’s absence become a silent veto. If someone will not discuss, set a temporary default with an opt-out: a fair rotation, a paid cleaner if everyone agrees and can afford it, or a clear minimum each person handles independently. Shared money and shared spaces still require consent, so do not impose costs unilaterally.

Finally, if repeated attempts fail, consider mediation or a conversation about whether the living arrangement still works. The practical goal is fewer repeated disputes and a way to revise the deal when schedules change, not perfect harmony.
COMMITMENTS
I take this to be primarily a coordination and communication problem, not a diagnosis of anyone’s character. My proposed first move is a visible, reviewable chore agreement plus a short recurring check-in; that depends on at least two flatmates being willing to try a low-cost structure and on no one vetoing all conversation. I would treat the avoiding friend’s absence as information to investigate, not as consent to any particular arrangement. If the trial does not reduce ambiguity, I would next consider a neutral facilitator or a discussion about changing the living arrangement; that step depends on lease terms, willingness, and whether anyone can afford to move or hire help. I am not assuming a cleaner is affordable, that all three want to stay, or that past resentment can be waved away. Unresolved: whether the avoidance stems from anxiety, resentment, schedule mismatch, or something outside the flat, and whether previous agreements have already made a new system feel punitive. A proposed test: for two weeks, use a shared board or calendar that defines each chore as outcome, deadline, and fallback, and hold a fifteen-minute weekly check-in; relevance is that it would show whether ambiguity or merely follow-through is the main obstacle. Success would be fewer “what did we agree” disputes and at least one missed task handled without a fight.
